machine.shared: A development machine, with other work running at times; the A/B runs are alternated for that reason

build.tls: OpenSSL 3.6.5 (bundled, static: linux-ext-libs 1.25); mbedTLS not built on this machine
build.note: CONFIG_DEBUG_TRACK_MEMORY is on (the .config of this machine): every allocation is tracked. A build without it does less work per allocation; that build was not measured here.

method.ab: Written on 2026-10-24, before the tag. 7.27.10 is the C code of the release: the main tree at cfe8bdc14 plus a 3-line patch to timeranger2.c that this study asked for (append_content() takes the system_flag the append already read, instead of reading it again from the topic json); the patch is committed before the tag. It is measured against 7.27.7, the last release with a study. 7.27.8 and 7.27.9 changed .c files only in modules/c/modbus and modules/c/mbus, and no measured binary links either (nm: 0 symbols of them in every benchmark and ctest binary), so their measured code is 7.27.7's and they were not built. 7.27.7 and 7.27.10 each built from a git worktree, with the same .config and compiler; outputs_ext shared (linux-ext-libs 1.25 at both). In each tree only the kernel libraries, the modules, performance/c/ and the three ctest binaries were built; perf_timeranger2 has not changed since 7.27.7. The two binaries of each benchmark run in rotation, the order turned every round, with a sync and a 3 s pause before each run (1 s for the three ctest binaries and the read phase): 8 rounds; 24 for perf_tr_treedb, perf_timeranger2, the TCP and TLS echo and both event loop echoes; 48 for the append test (the test_topic_pkey_integer chain) and for the read phase; perf_rotatory 16. The append test first measured 7.27.10 without the patch: -0.87% appends/s (t = -2.6) and -1.18% with a live reader (t = -2.8) after 48 rounds. An attribution A/B of that test with only timeranger2.c changed (7.27.7's against cfe8bdc14's, 24 rounds) placed it in commit 8d7e2a85f (-1.6%, t = -3.2; with a reader -2.0%, t = -4.0); forcing append_content() inline did not change it, and passing the system_flag removed it (+0.07%, t = 0.1). Every benchmark that appends was then measured again, both sides, with the patch: those are the figures of this report. Mean +- standard deviation (median), t = the change over its standard error; |t| < 3 is noise. The treedb figures are CPU time of the process per operation.
method.tag_run: The absolute figures of 7.27.10 are its side of the A/B run: its C code (cfe8bdc14 plus the system_flag patch), built on 2026-10-23/24 on the machine of the earlier reports. The per-second benchmarks drop their first and last second; reads page by page are the FORWARD pass. The binary sizes are those of the yunos built from the same tree.

story.title: Yuneta 7.27.10: a store that writes json text as it arrives
story.lead: 7.27.10 gives timeranger2 an append for a record that is already json text, `tranger2_append_record_text()`, and gobj-c a reader of the members of a json object from its text, `json_scan_object_members()`, with jansson's verdict and no node built. A writer of raw history that receives frames as text no longer parses each one whole to read three of its members and dumps it again to store it: db_events stores 2.2 times more frames per second on the same machine (24 700 -> 53 300), and on a Xeon E-2386G holds 20 000 records per second at 55% of one core. Against 7.27.7, the last release with a study, every one of the 41 figures stays inside its noise or gets faster: the appends of perf_timeranger2 are 1.6 to 2.9% faster. The study found, and the release fixes, a 1.6% loss of the json append that the split of the append had brought.

hero.text: frames stored per second by db_events with the text path: 53 300 against 24 700, the same source and the same SDK. On a production node (Xeon E-2386G) 20 000 records per second sustained for 10.5 minutes at 55% of a core, ~27.6 us a frame (was ~42).

tiles: treedb: update a node and save it
A page of 1 row, as a replica
story.append_note: -0.2% against 7.27.7 (225,670): t = -0.4 over 48 rounds, after the system_flag fix
story.ab_sub: Each benchmark built from the tree of each release (7.27.7 and 7.27.10; 7.27.8 and 7.27.9 changed no measured code), the binaries run in rotation: 8 rounds, 24 for the treedb writes, the store open and the echoes, 48 for the appends and the read path. A change inside its whisker is noise. Everything is on one axis: the change of the time an operation takes.
story.prices_sub: What got slower, how much, in which release, and what it buys.
story.no_prices: None. The one loss the study found, -1.6% of the json append (commit 8d7e2a85f: append_content() read the system_flag of the topic a second time), is fixed in the release and measured after the fix. Four figures sit at the edge of their noise without crossing it after 24 rounds, and their code did not change: the open of a store as a replica +1.1% (t = 2.8) and as the master +1.1% (t = 2.3), link or unlink +1.4% (t = 2.6), a tm query +1.5% (t = 2.2).
story.abs_sub: Absolute figures of the 7.27.10 build (its C code: the main tree before the version bump, with the system_flag fix), measured on 2026-10-23/24, before the tag, on the laptop above, as its side of the A/B run: one process, one core for the event loop (Yuneta scales by running one yuno per core). Mean of the rounds; the spread and the rounds are in the table at the end.

ab.case: 100 000 frames over TCP4H, each appended and acked
ab.label: db_events: frames stored and acked per second
ab.meaning: The writer of a raw history: what one yuno stores per second when frames arrive as json text.
ab.method: The same db_events source built twice against the SDK of this release: as it was (each frame parsed whole, its __md_trq__ deleted, dumped again by tranger2_append_record()) and with the text path (json_scan_object_members() reads id and __md_trq__ from the text, tranger2_append_record_text() writes it). Pinned to one CPU, a Python feeder on another, 100 000 frames of ~850 bytes, 4 alternated rounds.
ab.reason: The parse, the delete, the dump and the free of a frame of ~1 KB cost ~20 us; reading three members from its text costs 0.75 us (Xeon E-2386G). On a production node, 20 000 records per second on one server: db_events stores 19 906 frames/s sustained for 10.5 minutes at 55% of its core, ~27.6 us a frame (it was ~42 us, 77% of the core without keeping up), none lost, none duplicated in the steady state.
